question: Climate change: more than 1 200 Italian PGI and PDO products are at risk, including, in Sicily, Passito di Pantelleria, Ragusano, Pecorino Siciliano and the Limone di Siracusa (Syracuse lemon)

The concern about PGI (protection of geographical indication) and PDO (protected designation of origin) products in Italy, which are at risk because of climate change, is clearly reflected in the recent study commissioned by BonusFinder Italia. If, as expected, the planet warms by 0.79 degrees by 2040 and rainfall decreases by 0.

35 millimetres, some high-value Sicilian products such as the Ragusa PDO, the Pecorino PDO, and the Syracuse lemon could be seriously undermined. Sicily’s mild climate, which has made the island ideal for the production of citruses such as oranges and lemons, is now under threat. Animal husbandry and cheese production could be significantly affected, putting the region’s culinary heritage in jeopardy.

Crucial PDO products, such as Vastedda della Valle del Belice, could be particularly vulnerable. In the face of that challenge, action coordinated at EU level must be taken. In the light of the above: 1.
What measures will the Commission take to protect Sicilian PGI and PDO products at risk owing to climate change?
How will it support farming and food production in regions hit by changes of that kind?
What strategies could be pursued to ensure that Sicily’s rich culinary heritage is preserved and its designations of origin are protected?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.4.2024) EU support for agriculture and rural development is provided by the Rural Development Programme (RDP) of Sicily 2014-20221 and the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) Strategic Plan of Italy 2023-2027 (CSP)2. Italy may choose interventions in its RDP and CSP, that, among others, promote techniques addressing the climate situation and respect the environment.

The Sicilian RDP is the biggest regional RDP in Italy, having a total allocation of EUR 2.9 billion, of which EUR 0.8 billion still to be used. The Italian CSP has EUR 37 billion for the entire country (including almost EUR 3 billion for risk management3), and takes into account regional specificities. Geographical Indications (GIs) can play an important role in terms of sustainability.

Under the new regulation on GIs4, the Union's quality policy should respond to societal demands for production methods that are sustainable, environmentally and climate friendly, animal welfare ensuring, resource efficient and socially responsible. In this context producers are encouraged to adhere to sustainable practices that go beyond mandatory standards.
Such practices could be set out in the product specification5 or in a separate initiative.
1 Regulation (EU) No 1305/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 December 2013 on
support for rural development by the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development (EAFRD) and repealing Council Regulation (EC) No 1698/2005.

2 Regulation (EU) 2021/2115 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 2 December 2021 establishing rules on support for strategic plans to be drawn up by Member States under the common agricultural policy (CAP Strategic Plans) and financed by the European Agricultural Guarantee Fund (EAGF) and by the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development (EAFRD). 3 Article 76 of Regulation (EU) 2021/2115.

4 Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on geographical indications for wine, spirit drinks and agricultural products, as well as traditional specialities guaranteed and optional quality terms for agricultural products, amending Regulations (EU) No 1308/2013, (EU) 2019/787 and (EU) 2019/1753 and repealing Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 (P9_TC1-COD(2022)0089 Position of the European Parliament adopted at first reading on 28 February 2024 with a view to the adoption).

5 Sustainability practices contributing to environmental objectives should include climate change mitigation and adaptation, the conservation and sustainable use of soil, landscape, water and natural resources, the preservation of biodiversity, the conservation of rare seeds, local breeds and plant varieties, the promotion of short supply chains and the management and promotion of animal welfare.
